question_or_heading: Price is a number. Value is a judgment.
option_a: Price is whatever someone will pay right now — it can be pushed around by mood, urgency, or bad luck. Value is your own honest estimate of what a business is actually worth, based on the cash it can produce over time.

question_or_heading: Meet Mr. Market
option_a: Picture a business partner who knocks on your door every single day with a new price for your shares — sometimes cheerful and generous, sometimes gloomy and desperate. You're never obliged to trade with him. Some days you just say no thanks.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Intrinsic value = what a business is worth, independent of whatever its current price happens to say.

question_or_heading: Two identical push-carts sell the same tea recipe on the same street. One is priced at ₹2 lakh, the other at ₹3 lakh, just because its owner is short on cash and needs to sell fast. What does this tell you?
option_a: The ₹3 lakh cart must be the better business
option_b: Price can be pushed around by circumstances that have nothing to do with what the business is actually worth
option_c: Tea carts can't be valued at all
option_d: The cheaper cart is definitely a scam
hint: Think about what changed — the recipe and footfall, or just the seller's situation?
explanation: A seller's urgency, mood, or bad luck can move the price tag without changing anything about the cart's ovens, recipe, or footfall — that's the gap between price and value.

question_or_heading: “Intrinsic value” is best described as:
option_a: Whatever number is printed on today's price tag
option_b: What a business is actually worth, based on the cash it can generate over time
option_c: The size of a company's advertising budget
option_d: A rule that only applies to publicly listed companies
hint: Re-read the key phrase from this lesson's opening cards.
explanation: Intrinsic value looks past the sticker price and asks a harder question: how much cash can this business realistically produce, and for how long?

question_or_heading: Since price is easy to look up and value takes effort to estimate, most investors are better off just trusting the price.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Easy to find isn't the same as reliable.
explanation: Price is convenient, not correct. It reflects whatever the crowd feels this instant — which is a very different thing from what the business is worth.

question_or_heading: A news channel runs a scary headline and a stock drops 8% within an hour, even though nothing changed inside the company. What best explains this?
option_a: The company's factories and contracts shrank by 8% in that hour
option_b: Short-term price is driven by mood and headlines; the underlying business moves far more slowly
option_c: The stock exchange revalues every company hourly
option_d: This kind of thing never actually happens
hint: Could a factory or customer base really shrink 8% in sixty minutes?
explanation: Sentiment can swing in minutes. A factory, a customer base, a brand — none of that gets rebuilt that fast, which is exactly why price and value can drift apart.

question_or_heading: Benjamin Graham imagined the market as a business partner, ‘Mr. Market,’ who shows up daily with a new price. His point was:
option_a: You must trade with Mr. Market every day, or you're doing it wrong
option_b: You're free to ignore Mr. Market on the days his offer looks foolish, and act only when it favours you
option_c: Mr. Market is always rational, so always take his price
option_d: Mr. Market only appears once a year
hint: Remember — are you ever forced to say yes to him?
explanation: Mr. Market is moody — sometimes euphoric, sometimes gloomy. You're never obligated to trade with him; his silly offers are simply ones you walk past.

question_or_heading: The wider the gap, the safer your bet
option_a: When you buy well below your own honest estimate of worth, you build in a cushion. If your estimate turns out a little too optimistic, that cushion is what protects you.

question_or_heading: Quality isn't the whole story
option_a: A wonderful business bought at a foolish price can still be a poor investment. What you pay relative to what you get is the entire game — not just how good the business is.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Margin of safety = the cushion between what you pay and what you honestly believe something is worth.

question_or_heading: You estimate a snack-stall chain is worth about ₹10 lakh. Mr. Market offers it to you at ₹7 lakh today. The sensible move is to:
option_a: Refuse, because a discount always means something is wrong
option_b: Take the offer seriously — buying below your own honest estimate is exactly when Mr. Market is worth listening to
option_c: Wait for Mr. Market to raise the price first
option_d: Ignore price entirely and only look at value
hint: Is this one of the days Mr. Market's price actually favours you?
explanation: This is the whole point of the Mr. Market idea: his usefulness shows up on the days his price sits below what you believe the business is really worth.

question_or_heading: Your estimate of worth is ₹500/share. You buy at ₹350/share. Roughly how big is your margin of safety?
hint: Find the gap first, then divide it by the value estimate — not the price paid.
explanation: ₹500 − ₹350 = ₹150, and ₹150 ÷ ₹500 = 30%. That gap is your cushion if your estimate turns out to be a little optimistic.

question_or_heading: “Margin of safety” exists mainly to protect you from:
option_a: Paying brokerage fees
option_b: Your own estimate of value being wrong
option_c: The company changing its logo
option_d: Having to file taxes
hint: It's not about fees, logos, or paperwork — think about where the real uncertainty lives.
explanation: No one's value estimate is perfect. Buying with a cushion below that estimate means small errors don't sink you.

question_or_heading: A falling share price is always proof that a business is getting worse.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Could fear, forced selling, or market-wide panic move a price with the business untouched?
explanation: Prices fall for plenty of reasons unrelated to the business — sector-wide fear, forced selling, a bad quarter for the whole market. The business itself may be untouched.

question_or_heading: Two friends each buy the same excellent bakery chain. Rina pays 12× its yearly profit; Dev pays 40×. A year later, both bakeries perform identically. Whose investment is more likely to disappoint?
option_a: Rina's — she paid too little
option_b: Dev's — he paid a price that already assumed years of growth that may not show up
option_c: Neither — price paid never matters
option_d: Both equally, since it's the same bakery
hint: Same business, same results — so what's actually different between Rina and Dev?
explanation: A wonderful business bought at a foolish price can still be a poor investment. What you pay relative to what you get is the whole game.

question_or_heading: A rupee today beats a rupee tomorrow
option_a: Money in hand right now can be invested and start growing immediately. That earning window is the entire reason sooner is worth more than later — this idea is called the time value of money.

question_or_heading: Compounding vs. simple interest
option_a: Simple interest only ever pays on your original amount. Compound interest pays interest on the interest you've already earned too — which is why growth accelerates the longer you wait.

question_or_heading: Discounting runs the clock backward
option_a: To find what a future rupee is worth today, you shrink it using a discount rate. The higher the rate, the smaller that future amount looks in today's money.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Rule of 72: divide 72 by the annual growth rate to estimate how many years money takes to double.

question_or_heading: Your uncle offers you ₹1,00,000 today, or ₹1,00,000 in five years. Which should you prefer, and why?
option_a: Either — it's the same amount
option_b: Today — money in hand now can be invested and start growing immediately
option_c: In five years — money left untouched always becomes more valuable on its own
option_d: In five years, to avoid the responsibility of managing it
hint: What could you do with the money in the meantime?
explanation: Money today can be put to work right away. That earning window is the entire reason sooner is worth more than later.

question_or_heading: ₹10,000 is invested at 10% annual compound interest. What is it worth after 2 years (roughly)?
hint: Grow it by 10% once, then grow that new total by 10% again.
explanation: Year 1: ₹10,000 × 1.10 = ₹11,000. Year 2: ₹11,000 × 1.10 = ₹12,100. The second year's interest is earned on the first year's interest too — that's compounding.

question_or_heading: “Discounting” a future cash flow means:
option_a: Applying a retail markdown to it
option_b: Converting a future rupee amount into its equivalent worth in today's rupees
option_c: Deleting it from your calculations
option_d: Adding a bonus for good luck
hint: It's the mirror image of compounding — working backward from the future.
explanation: Discounting runs the compounding logic backward: it asks what amount today would grow into that future number, at a chosen rate of return.

question_or_heading: Two analysts value the same ₹1,00,000 cash flow arriving in 5 years. Anaya uses a 6% discount rate, Vikram uses a 12% rate. Whose present-value estimate comes out lower?
option_a: Anaya's
option_b: Vikram's
option_c: They must be equal
option_d: Impossible to say
hint: A bigger discount rate shrinks the future faster.
explanation: A higher discount rate shrinks future money faster — you're demanding more return for waiting, so the same future amount is worth less to you today.

question_or_heading: Simple interest and compound interest give you the same result over multiple years.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does simple interest ever pay interest on interest already earned?
explanation: Simple interest only ever pays on the original amount. Compound interest pays interest on the interest too, so it pulls ahead more and more each year.

question_or_heading: The “Rule of 72” is a quick trick to estimate how long money takes to double. At 9% annual growth, roughly how many years until it doubles?
option_a: 4 years
option_b: 6 years
option_c: 8 years
option_d: 12 years
explanation: 72 ÷ 9 = 8. Divide 72 by the annual growth rate and you get a rough doubling time — handy for gut-checking compounding without a calculator.

question_or_heading: Everything owned must be paid for by something
option_a: A balance sheet always balances: what a business owns (assets) was funded either by what it owes others (liabilities) or by the owner's own stake (equity).

question_or_heading: Assets vs. liabilities
option_a: Assets are things the business owns or controls that hold economic value — cash, equipment, a delivery scooter. Liabilities are obligations it must eventually settle — loans, unpaid bills.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Equity = Assets − Liabilities — what's actually left over for the owner once every debt is accounted for.

question_or_heading: Meera's Tiffin Service owns a delivery scooter, a rented kitchen deposit, and ₹50,000 cash — ₹1,00,000 in assets altogether. It owes ₹20,000 to a supplier. What is her equity?
option_c: The scooter's price alone
option_d: Impossible to know
hint: Start from total assets, then subtract what's owed.
explanation: Assets − Liabilities = Equity. ₹1,00,000 in assets minus ₹20,000 owed leaves ₹80,000 — what's actually hers once the debt is settled.

question_or_heading: Which of these belongs on the “assets” side of a balance sheet?
option_a: A loan owed to the bank
option_b: Unpaid supplier bills
option_c: The delivery scooter the business owns
option_d: Retained losses from a bad year
hint: Assets are things the business owns or controls.
explanation: Assets are things the business owns or controls that hold economic value — a scooter it can use or sell qualifies. Loans and unpaid bills sit on the opposite side of the ledger.

question_or_heading: Which of these belongs on the “liabilities” side?
option_a: Cash in the till
option_b: A supplier invoice not yet paid
option_c: The kitchen equipment
option_d: Owner's equity
hint: Liabilities are what the business owes to someone else.
explanation: An unpaid invoice is money the business owes someone else — a liability, by definition.

question_or_heading: The fundamental balance sheet equation is:
option_a: Revenue − Expenses = Profit
option_b: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
option_c: Price = Earnings × Multiple
option_d: Cash + Debt = Value
hint: This is this lesson's key phrase, rearranged.
explanation: Every rupee of assets was funded either by what the business owes others (liabilities) or by the owner's own stake (equity) — the two sides always balance.

question_or_heading: A business can own a large pile of assets and still be in real trouble, if its liabilities are even larger.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Size of assets alone doesn't tell you what's left over.
explanation: Size of assets alone tells you little. What matters is the gap left over after liabilities — that gap is equity, and it can be thin, or even negative.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: Valuers lean on three lenses
option_a: The Asset Approach asks what the business owns. The Market Approach asks what similar businesses sold for. The Income Approach asks what it's likely to earn in the future. Most real valuations blend more than one.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: EBITDA strips out the noise
option_a: Removing interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization from earnings lets you compare operating profitability across companies, even when they're financed or depreciate their equipment very differently.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Book Value = Total Assets − Total Liabilities — a useful floor, but it mostly ignores goodwill, often a business's biggest hidden asset.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: Professional valuers generally lean on three broad approaches. Which trio is it?
option_a: Guesswork, gut feeling, and negotiation
option_b: The Asset Approach, the Market Approach, and the Income Approach
option_c: Stock charts, news headlines, and social media buzz
option_d: Tax filings, payroll, and inventory counts
hint: Think: what it owns, what similar businesses sold for, what it's likely to earn.
explanation: These three — what it owns, what similar businesses sold for, and what it's likely to earn — are the pillars most valuation professionals build on.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: The Asset Approach values a business mainly by:
option_a: Adding up the fair market value of what it owns and subtracting what it owes
option_b: Comparing its share price to rival companies
option_c: Forecasting ten years of future profit
option_d: Counting its social media followers
hint: The name is a clue — it's about what's on the shelves, not the future.
explanation: It's essentially: value everything the business holds at fair market value, then subtract liabilities — what's left is the net asset value.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: A young food-delivery startup has no profit yet but plenty of orders coming in. Which Market Approach ratio would still work for it?
option_a: Price-to-earnings ratio (needs profit to exist)
option_b: Price-to-revenue ratio — revenue exists even without profit
option_c: Book value of its office chairs
option_d: None — unprofitable companies can never be valued
hint: Which of these two things does the startup actually have: profit, or revenue?
explanation: Price-to-revenue is popular for young or fast-growing companies precisely because revenue shows up long before profit does.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: The Income Approach is built around one core idea: a business is worth
option_a: Whatever its founder believes it's worth
option_b: The future cash it's expected to generate, converted into today's money
option_c: The total salary of its employees
option_d: The price of its most expensive machine
hint: This connects straight back to present value from the last lesson.
explanation: This is present value in action — project the future benefit stream, then discount it back to what that stream is worth right now.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: EBITDA strips out interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization from earnings mainly so that:
option_a: The company pays less tax
option_b: Analysts can compare operating profitability across companies without financing or accounting choices distorting the picture
option_c: The numbers look bigger for investors
option_d: It replaces the need for a balance sheet
hint: It's about fair comparison, not about looking impressive.
explanation: Two companies can run near-identical operations but look very different once you factor in how each is financed or depreciates its equipment — EBITDA strips that noise out.

lesson_title: Three Ways to Value a Business
question_or_heading: Book Value (Total Assets − Total Liabilities) is usually treated as a floor rather than a full answer. Why?
option_a: It's illegal to rely on it fully
option_b: It leans on historic, depreciated figures and largely ignores goodwill — often a business's biggest intangible asset
option_c: It always overstates a company's worth
option_d: Only banks are allowed to calculate it
hint: Think about what accounting numbers leave out — brand, relationships, reputation.
explanation: Book value leans on historical accounting numbers and mostly ignores brand, customer relationships, and other goodwill — useful as a sanity-check floor, rarely the full story.

question_or_heading: Two philosophies, one goal
option_a: Value-minded investors hunt for businesses priced below what they're worth today. Growth-minded investors bet on how much bigger a business will become — and are willing to pay more now for a bigger future.

question_or_heading: Growth needs a bigger leap of faith
option_a: The further out your assumptions reach, the more today's price depends on the future actually arriving on schedule.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: A high price isn't automatically foolish, and a low price isn't automatically safe — the real question is always price against what's realistically ahead.

question_or_heading: Which statement best describes a “growth” approach to investing?
option_a: Paying a premium today because you expect much larger profits down the line
option_b: Buying only companies that carry zero debt
option_c: Avoiding every technology company on principle
option_d: Refusing to ever sell a position
hint: Think about what growth investors are betting will happen.
explanation: Growth investing accepts a higher price today in exchange for a bet on faster future expansion.

question_or_heading: A retailer trades at 8× profit; a software company trades at 45× profit. This gap most likely reflects:
option_a: The software company is committing fraud
option_b: The market expects the software company's profits to grow much faster
option_c: Retailers are always mispriced
option_d: Multiples are handed out randomly
hint: Multiples often price in expectations, not just today's numbers.
explanation: Higher multiples often reflect higher expected growth — investors are paying today for profits they expect years from now.

question_or_heading: A “value” label on a stock guarantees it's a safe investment.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Could a stock look cheap for a very good reason?
explanation: Cheap on paper doesn't mean safe. A company can be statistically cheap because it's genuinely troubled — a classic ‘value trap.’

question_or_heading: What is a “value trap”?
option_a: A legal clause used in mergers
option_b: A stock that looks statistically cheap but is cheap because the underlying business is genuinely deteriorating
option_c: A discount offered directly by a stockbroker
option_d: A term with no real meaning
hint: Think of a stock that looks like a bargain but isn't.
explanation: A value trap is priced low for good reason — the business itself may be shrinking or struggling, so the apparent discount is a mirage.

question_or_heading: Why does a growth-oriented purchase typically demand more forecasting than a value-oriented one?
option_a: Growth companies are required to file more paperwork
option_b: More of the expected payoff sits further out in time, so more years must be predicted correctly
option_c: Growth companies don't publish financial statements
option_d: It doesn't — both require identical forecasting
hint: Where does most of the expected payoff sit — near-term, or years away?
explanation: When most of a company's expected value comes from profits several years away, small changes in those far-off assumptions swing the valuation a lot.

question_or_heading: No free lunch
option_a: Higher potential return usually comes bundled with higher potential pain. Understanding that trade-off is the beginning of managing risk sensibly.

question_or_heading: Risk wears more than one face
option_a: It can mean losing money permanently, being unable to sell an asset when you need to (liquidity risk), or having one bad surprise wipe out a bet that was never spread around.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Return is what you hope for. Risk is what you plan for.

question_or_heading: Why do riskier investments generally need to offer higher expected returns to attract buyers?
option_a: Riskier investments are illegal without a return premium
option_b: To compensate investors for the extra chance of losing money
option_c: Government rules require it in every market
option_d: They don't — risk and return are unrelated
hint: Why would anyone accept extra uncertainty for nothing extra in return?
explanation: Investors demand extra expected reward for bearing extra uncertainty — otherwise there'd be no reason to take the risk at all.

question_or_heading: A fixed deposit paying 6% and a small startup offering a possible 40% return illustrate:
option_a: The startup is obviously the better choice
option_b: A basic risk-return trade-off — the higher potential payout comes bundled with meaningfully higher odds of loss
option_c: Fixed deposits are always a foolish choice
option_d: The numbers must be fabricated
hint: Why might that 40% not be a sure thing?
explanation: The startup's higher potential payoff exists precisely because its odds of failure are much higher too.

question_or_heading: Putting your entire savings into one stock is a low-risk strategy, as long as you believe strongly in the company.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does belief change what happens if one piece of bad news hits?
explanation: Concentrating everything in one bet means a single piece of bad news can do outsized damage — conviction doesn't remove that exposure.

question_or_heading: “Liquidity risk” refers to:
option_a: The risk that a company mismanages its cash reserves
option_b: The risk that you can't sell an investment quickly without accepting a much lower price
option_c: The risk of interest rates changing
option_d: A risk that applies only to real estate
hint: Think about what happens when you actually try to exit an investment.
explanation: Some investments are hard to exit quickly at a fair price — that inability to sell on your own timeline is liquidity risk.

question_or_heading: Which of these is a sensible response to risk, rather than an attempt to pretend it doesn't exist?
option_a: Avoiding all investing, forever
option_b: Spreading money across different bets that don't all fail for the same reason
option_c: Borrowing heavily to concentrate on one stock
option_d: Ignoring risk since it can't be perfectly measured
hint: Think about what happens to a portfolio when bad news hits only one of many holdings.
explanation: Risk can rarely be eliminated, but diversifying across bets that don't all fail together can reduce how hard any single mistake hurts.

question_or_heading: Profit on paper isn't cash in hand
option_a: A company can report a profit and still run low on cash, because profit includes non-cash items and ignores money tied up in day-to-day operations.

question_or_heading: ‘Free’ means left over after the essentials
option_a: Free cash flow is the cash generated by operations, minus what's needed to maintain and grow the business's physical assets.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Free Cash Flow = Cash from Operations − Capital Expenditure.

question_or_heading: Free cash flow is best described as:
option_a: Total revenue collected in a year
option_b: The cash left over after a business covers its operating costs and needed spending on equipment or property
option_c: The cash sitting in the founder's personal account
option_d: A made-up figure with no real formula
hint: Think about what's actually free to be paid out or reinvested elsewhere.
explanation: It's the cash actually free to be paid out, reinvested elsewhere, or saved — after the business has funded what it needs to keep running.

question_or_heading: A company reports ₹10 crore net profit but spends ₹12 crore replacing aging machinery that same year. Which number better reflects its real cash position?
option_a: Net profit alone
option_b: Free cash flow, which accounts for that spending
option_c: Neither number is informative
option_d: The company's share price
hint: One of these two numbers ignores that ₹12 crore entirely.
explanation: Net profit ignores the cash actually spent on new machinery; free cash flow captures it, which is why the two figures can tell very different stories.

question_or_heading: A business can look profitable on its income statement and still run out of cash.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does profit account for money tied up in unpaid customer invoices?
explanation: Profit includes non-cash accounting entries and ignores things like money tied up in unpaid invoices — cash can run short even while profit looks healthy.

question_or_heading: “Capital expenditure” (CapEx) refers to:
option_a: Everyday office snacks and supplies
option_b: Spending on long-lived assets like machinery, buildings, or equipment
option_c: Employee salaries
option_d: Marketing spend only
hint: Think long-lived, not day-to-day.
explanation: CapEx covers money spent on assets expected to be useful for years, like machinery or property — a direct input into the free cash flow formula.

question_or_heading: Why do many valuation approaches focus on free cash flow rather than net profit?
option_a: Free cash flow is easier to manipulate
option_b: Free cash flow better reflects the cash actually available to owners after necessary reinvestment
option_c: Net profit is not permitted in valuation work
option_d: There's no meaningful difference between the two
hint: Think about accounting noise versus actual spendable cash.
explanation: Free cash flow strips out accounting noise and shows what's truly left for owners after the business reinvests what it needs to keep going.

question_or_heading: The most common shortcut in investing
option_a: The Price-to-Earnings ratio compares what you pay for a share to how much profit that share represents — a fast, rough gauge used everywhere.

question_or_heading: A starting question, not a final answer
option_a: A low P/E can mean a bargain — or a business the market has good reason to doubt. The number alone never tells you which.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: P/E = Share Price ÷ Earnings per Share.

question_or_heading: A company's share trades at ₹200, with earnings per share of ₹10. What is its P/E ratio?
hint: Divide price by earnings per share.
explanation: ₹200 ÷ ₹10 = 20. You're effectively paying 20 times the company's current annual profit for one share.

question_or_heading: A very low P/E ratio, on its own, most likely means:
option_a: The company is definitely a great buy, no further checking needed
option_b: It could be a genuine bargain, or a sign the market has real doubts about the business — it's a starting clue, not a conclusion
option_c: P/E ratios below 10 are against exchange rules
option_d: A low P/E always signals imminent bankruptcy
hint: One number rarely settles the question by itself.
explanation: A low P/E is a prompt to investigate further, not an automatic verdict — cheap for a good reason and cheap for a bad reason can look identical on this one number.

question_or_heading: P/E ratios are equally meaningful when comparing companies from completely different industries.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Do all industries share similar growth rates and capital needs?
explanation: Different industries carry very different typical P/E levels because of different growth rates, capital needs, and risk profiles — comparing within the same industry is far more useful.

question_or_heading: If a company's earnings are expected to grow quickly, investors will often accept:
option_a: A lower P/E than slower-growing peers
option_b: A higher P/E than slower-growing peers, since they're partly paying for future growth too
option_c: No P/E ratio at all
option_d: A P/E fixed at exactly 15 by convention
hint: Think about what a higher multiple is really paying for.
explanation: Faster expected growth usually justifies paying more per rupee of today's earnings, since tomorrow's earnings are expected to be bigger.

question_or_heading: Which kind of company would typically show a meaningful P/E ratio at all?
option_a: A company with zero or negative earnings
option_b: A profitable company with positive earnings per share
option_c: Any company, regardless of profit
option_d: Only companies that pay dividends
hint: The formula needs a positive number on the bottom.
explanation: P/E requires positive earnings to make sense — companies with no profit show a meaningless or undefined P/E, which is one reason price-to-revenue exists as an alternative.

question_or_heading: A scoreboard for a stretch of time
option_a: Where the balance sheet is a snapshot at one moment, the income statement tracks what happened over a period — usually a quarter or a year.

question_or_heading: Follow the money down the page
option_a: Revenue arrives first, then costs get subtracted step by step, until what's left at the very bottom is net profit.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Revenue − costs of every kind = profit, one line at a time.

question_or_heading: On an income statement, “Revenue” refers to:
option_a: Profit remaining after all costs
option_b: The total money earned from selling goods or services, before any costs are subtracted
option_c: Cash currently sitting in the bank
option_d: The value of unsold inventory
hint: It's the very first line, before anything is subtracted.
explanation: Revenue is the top line — the full amount earned from sales, before a single cost has been deducted yet.

question_or_heading: “Cost of Goods Sold” (COGS) typically includes:
option_a: Office rent for company headquarters
option_b: The direct costs of producing what was sold, like raw materials and factory labour
option_c: Marketing campaigns
option_d: Executive salaries
hint: Think about costs tied directly to making the product.
explanation: COGS covers the direct costs tied to making or delivering the product itself — separate from overhead like marketing or admin.

question_or_heading: Revenue minus COGS gives you:
option_a: Net profit
option_b: Gross profit
option_c: Operating profit
option_d: EBITDA
hint: This is the first profit checkpoint on the statement.
explanation: Revenue − COGS = Gross Profit, the first profit checkpoint, before operating expenses like marketing and admin are subtracted.

question_or_heading: Which of these typically comes last on an income statement?
option_a: Revenue
option_b: Gross profit
option_c: Operating profit
option_d: Net profit
hint: Think about which checkpoint accounts for every single expense.
explanation: The statement builds downward from revenue through several profit checkpoints, ending at net profit — the true bottom line after every expense, interest, and tax.
